{
  "need": "Status",
  "secondary": { "name": "Identity" },
  "read": "When a newer hire outperforms their manager in a visible skill, the status dynamic runs both ways: they need to feel that competence is recognized and respected, not quietly managed or minimized. If they sense you pulling rank to compensate, they will disengage or start working around you. The identity piece is that they are still figuring out who they are professionally, and having a strength that exceeds yours is a formative moment that can either build loyalty or breed resentment depending on how you handle it.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Enforcer", "instinct": "Overload them with tasks outside their strong area, quietly sideline their strength, or remind them of hierarchy to restore the balance of power, which signals insecurity and erodes their respect for you." },
  "mentorMove": "Name the gap openly, honor it as an asset to the team, and reframe the relationship as two people with different strengths working toward shared goals. Your job is not to be the best at everything; it is to make the team better, and leveraging their skill while coaching their development is exactly how you do that.",
  "holdFirm": [
    "The standard for professionalism, collaboration, and accountability does not shift because they are skilled.",
    "Their technical edge does not exempt them from doing the less glamorous parts of the role.",
    "You still set direction, context, and standards even when they execute better."
  ],
  "stayFlexible": [
    "Let them lead in the area where they are stronger and give them visible credit for it.",
    "Shift your coaching toward the areas where they are still developing rather than the area where they have surpassed you.",
    "Create genuine opportunities for them to teach you or the broader team, which honors their competence and builds belonging."
  ],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 2, "label": "Questions" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "I want to have a straight conversation with you about how we work together, because I think we are in an interesting position and I would rather name it than pretend it is not there." },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "You have picked up this part of the work faster than most people I have seen, including me at your stage. I am curious how you are experiencing that, because I imagine it creates some awkward moments when you can see a better path than the one I am taking." },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "Here is how I want to think about this together: your strength in this area is genuinely useful to me and to the team, and I want to use it, not manage around it. Where I need your partnership is in the bigger picture stuff, the context, the client relationships, the parts that come with time, and I can actually help you build those. So let us be deliberate about who leads what and why." },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "I am holding you to a high standard across the full role, not just the part you have mastered, because I know you are capable of being strong across all of it. And I will tell you clearly when you are meeting that bar and when you are not. I am in your corner on this, and I think you have a real ceiling ahead of you if we work it right." }
  ],
  "longGame": "A manager who can say out loud that a direct report is better at something, and then build a structure that uses that, earns durable loyalty and shapes how that person thinks about leadership for the rest of their career. The goal is that when they eventually manage someone who outpaces them, they already know what good looks like."
}
situation: My newest hire is better at part of the job than I am and we both know it.
